topics.name: Election of 1824
topics.kicker: Jackson wins the most votes, but the House picks Adams · The “corrupt bargain”
topics.dates: Voting in late 1824; House vote February 9, 1825
topics.briefing: In 1824, four candidates from the same party ran for president: Andrew Jackson, John Quincy Adams, William Crawford, and Henry Clay. Jackson won the most popular and electoral votes but not a majority, so under the Twelfth Amendment the House of Representatives chose among the top three. It picked Adams in February 1825, and when Adams named Clay secretary of state, Jackson and his supporters called it a “corrupt bargain.”
topics.answerHtml: Election of 1824 (or 1824 presidential election; prompt on presidential election or the “corrupt bargain”; do not accept other years, such as 1825 or 1828)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a famous story, New York congressman Stephen Van Rensselaer [“van REN-suh-leer”] bowed his head in prayer during the deciding vote for this contest, saw a ballot lying on the floor, and took it as a sign. His vote swung his state and gave the winner the thirteenth state he needed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election that the House of Representatives decided in February 1825 by choosing John Quincy Adams.

tossups.p: During this campaign, newspapers printed some of the first known opinion polls, informal “straw polls” of voters, which showed a Tennessee war hero in the lead. That candidate went on to win more popular votes than any of his three rivals.
tossups.r: But the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams instead. For 10 points, name this presidential election.

tossups.p: Kentucky’s legislature told the state’s congressmen to vote for a Tennessean in the deciding round of this contest, but most of them chose a New Englander backed by their fellow Kentuckian, the Speaker of the House. That Speaker had finished fourth in electoral votes.
tossups.r: He then became secretary of state. For 10 points, name this election that led to charges of a “corrupt bargain.”

tossups.p: A poorly attended meeting of congressmen nominated a Georgia candidate in this contest, the last time a party relied on that “King Caucus” method. That candidate, the secretary of the Treasury, was backed by Martin Van Buren but had suffered a serious stroke the year before.
tossups.r: He was William Crawford. For 10 points, name this four-way presidential election won by John Quincy Adams.

tossups.p: Because no candidate won a majority of electoral votes in this contest, an amendment ratified in 1804 required the House to choose among the top three finishers, with each state’s delegation casting one vote. That rule left out the fourth-place finisher, Henry Clay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which the House chose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: John C. Calhoun dropped out of the presidential race in this contest and ran for vice president instead, winning that office easily with support from two rival camps. No candidate for president, however, won a majority of the electoral votes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: In the deciding vote for this contest, held on February 9, 1825, one candidate won thirteen state delegations, another won seven, and William Crawford won four. Each state’s delegation in the House of Representatives cast a single vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which John Quincy Adams defeated Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: After this contest, one candidate called his Kentucky rival “the Judas of the West,” comparing him to the disciple who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. That rival had just been named secretary of state by the winner.
tossups.r: The man who made that charge, Andrew Jackson, had won the most popular votes. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: Months after losing this contest, one candidate resigned from the U.S. Senate, and the Tennessee legislature nominated him for the next presidential race. His supporters began campaigning for that rematch almost at once.
tossups.r: That candidate, Andrew Jackson, won the rematch in 1828. For 10 points, name the earlier election that he lost to John Quincy Adams.

tossups.p: This contest helped break apart the only national party of its time, the Democratic-Republicans. Supporters of its loser formed what became the Democratic Party, while backers of its winner and his secretary of state became known as National Republicans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election decided by the House, in which John Quincy Adams beat Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: This contest ended the so-called Era of Good Feelings, when only one major party competed for the presidency. All four main candidates belonged to that party, and one of them was Speaker of the House at the time.
tossups.r: Another, John Quincy Adams, won the presidency in the House. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: The winner of this contest is the only person to become president after finishing second in both the popular vote and the electoral vote. He had served for nearly eight years as secretary of state under James Monroe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this election in which John Quincy Adams defeated Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: In this contest, six of the twenty-four states still let their legislatures choose presidential electors instead of holding a popular vote. A general who had won the Battle of New Orleans led the popular vote with about 41 percent.
tossups.r: That general, Andrew Jackson, still lost to John Quincy Adams in the House. For 10 points, name this election.

tossups.p: In January 1825, the fourth-place finisher in this contest met privately for hours with a rival who shared his support for tariffs, roads, and canals, and then backed that rival in the House. Opponents claimed the two men had made a deal.
tossups.r: That claimed deal became known as the “corrupt bargain.” For 10 points, name this election that sent John Quincy Adams to the White House.

tossups.p: The Tennessee legislature nominated one candidate for this contest two years early, in 1822, and elected him to the U.S. Senate the next year. That candidate was a hero of the War of 1812 who had won the Battle of New Orleans.
tossups.r: He won the most votes but lost in the House. For 10 points, name this election in which Andrew Jackson lost to John Quincy Adams.

clues.t: Four Democratic-Republicans ran: Andrew Jackson, John Quincy Adams, William Crawford, and Henry Clay
No one won a majority of electoral votes, so the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams in February 1825
Adams named Henry Clay secretary of state, and Jackson’s supporters called it a “corrupt bargain”
Andrew Jackson won the most popular votes (about 41 percent) and the most electoral votes (99) but lost
Under the 12th Amendment (1804), the House chose among the top three, with one vote per state delegation
Henry Clay finished fourth in electoral votes, so the House could not pick him; as Speaker, he helped Adams win
Electoral votes: Jackson 99, Adams 84, Crawford 41, Clay 37; a majority took 131
The House vote on February 9, 1825: Adams 13 states, Jackson 7, Crawford 4
Jackson resigned from the Senate, was renominated by Tennessee in 1825, and beat Adams in their 1828 rematch
John C. Calhoun won the vice presidency easily, backed by both the Adams and Jackson camps
Ended the Era of Good Feelings; the Democratic-Republicans split into Jackson’s Democrats and the National Republicans
Stephen Van Rensselaer said he saw a ballot on the floor while praying, then voted for Adams, swinging New York
A poorly attended congressional caucus (“King Caucus”) nominated Crawford, the last nomination made that way
Treasury Secretary William Crawford of Georgia had suffered a serious stroke in 1823
Martin Van Buren backed Crawford, then helped build the Jackson coalition that became the Democratic Party
Kentucky’s legislature told its congressmen to vote for Jackson, but most of them voted for Adams
Jackson called Clay “the Judas of the West”
Newspapers printed some of the first known opinion polls (“straw polls”) during the campaign
Adams is the only president who finished second in both the popular vote and the electoral vote
Six of the 24 states still had their legislatures choose electors instead of holding a popular vote
Tennessee’s legislature nominated Jackson in 1822 and elected him to the U.S. Senate in 1823
In January 1825, Clay met privately with Adams for hours before backing him

trap.title: Name the right year
trap.body: Election tossups describe the candidates but want the year. The House settled this race in February 1825, and Jackson beat Adams in their 1828 rematch, so “1825” and “1828” are both wrong. “Corrupt bargain” earns only a prompt here: it names the deal that Jackson’s supporters said came after the election, not the election itself, so you still owe the year.
trap.fix: Four candidates, William Crawford, the House picking the president, and Clay becoming secretary of state all mean 1824. Jackson defeating Adams, the Coffin Handbills, and the Tariff of Abominations mean 1828. If the moderator prompts after “corrupt bargain,” say “1824.”
trap.line: Real answer line: United States presidential election of 1824 (prompt on presidential election or “corrupt bargain”; do not accept other years)

topics.name: Elizabeth Warren
topics.kicker: U.S. senator from Massachusetts, first elected 2012 · Ran for president in 2020
topics.dates: Born 1949; elected to the Senate in 2012
topics.briefing: Elizabeth Warren grew up in Oklahoma, won a college scholarship for debate, and became a law professor who studied why families go bankrupt, eventually teaching at Harvard Law School. In 2007 she proposed a new government agency to oversee loans, credit cards, and other financial products, an idea that became the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. In 2012 she became the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from Massachusetts, and she ran for president in 2020.
topics.answerHtml: Elizabeth Warren (accept Elizabeth Ann Warren or Elizabeth Ann Herring; prompt on Elizabeth; do not accept “Earl Warren”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: With her daughter, this law professor wrote _The Two-Income Trap_, a 2003 book about why many middle-class families with two working parents were going broke. Years earlier, she had helped write a book-length study of Americans who filed for bankruptcy.
tossups.r: She later won a U.S. Senate seat in Massachusetts in 2012. For 10 points, name this senator who ran for president in 2020.

tossups.p: In a 2007 article titled “Unsafe at Any Rate,” this law professor argued that loans and credit cards should be checked for safety, just as toasters are, by a new government agency. That idea was written into the Dodd–Frank Act of 2010.
tossups.r: The agency became the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator, first elected in 2012.

tossups.p: In February 2017, the Senate voted to stop this senator from speaking during a debate over Jeff Sessions’s nomination for attorney general, after she read aloud a 1986 letter by Coretta Scott King. Majority Leader Mitch McConnell explained, “She was warned. She was given an explanation.”
tossups.r: His next words, “Nevertheless, she persisted,” became a widely repeated slogan. For 10 points, name this senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: After the 2008 financial crisis, this law professor chaired a Congressional Oversight Panel that kept watch on the Troubled Asset Relief Program, the government’s rescue of the banks. In 2010 and 2011, she worked for President Barack Obama setting up a new consumer agency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who first proposed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and later became a senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Born in Oklahoma City, this future politician won a debate scholarship to George Washington University at age 16. She left college to get married and later finished a degree in speech pathology at the University of Houston.
tossups.r: She went on to teach law at Harvard. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator who ran for president in 2020.

tossups.p: This expert on bankruptcy law taught at the University of Texas and the University of Pennsylvania before joining the faculty of Harvard Law School in the 1990s. She had earned her own law degree at Rutgers in 1976.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law professor who later became a Democratic senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: In 2012, this candidate defeated Republican Scott Brown, who had won a 2010 special election for the Senate seat long held by Ted Kennedy. That win made her the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from her state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat from Massachusetts who later ran for president in 2020.

tossups.p: This candidate launched a 2019 presidential campaign at a mill in Lawrence, Massachusetts, where textile workers had gone on strike in 1912 in the “Bread and Roses” strike. Her campaign became known for the phrase “I have a plan for that.”
tossups.r: She ended that campaign in March 2020. For 10 points, name this senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: This future senator was registered as a Republican until 1996 and has said she once thought that party best supported free markets. Her research on families in debt later led her to call for stronger rules on lenders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democratic senator from Massachusetts, a former Harvard law professor.

tossups.p: This politician wrote the memoir _A Fighting Chance_ in 2014 and titled a 2021 book _Persist_, after words used about her on the Senate floor. Her other books include _This Fight Is Our Fight_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator who first proposed the idea for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

tossups.p: In 2011, Barack Obama picked Richard Cordray, not this official, to be the first director of a new agency she had spent a year setting up. Two months later, she announced that she would run for the U.S. Senate.
tossups.r: That agency is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. For 10 points, name this senator first elected in 2012.

tossups.p: Before going to law school, this woman taught children with disabilities at a public school in New Jersey, after earning a degree in speech pathology. She later spent decades teaching and writing about bankruptcy law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Harvard law professor who was elected to the Senate from Massachusetts in 2012.

tossups.p: This senator was reelected in 2018 over Geoff Diehl and in 2024 over John Deaton, both Republicans. Before entering politics, she had spent more than thirty years as a law professor, much of that time studying bankruptcy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democratic senator from Massachusetts who taught at Harvard Law School.

tossups.p: While this future politician was growing up in Oklahoma, her father had a heart attack, and her mother took a minimum-wage job at Sears to help keep the family’s house. She has often told that story when talking about working families.
tossups.r: She later became a law professor at Harvard. For 10 points, name this senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: During the 2020 race, this candidate proposed a yearly “wealth tax” on households worth more than $50 million, one of many detailed plans her campaign released. She ended that campaign in March 2020, soon after the Super Tuesday primaries.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator who first proposed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

clues.t: Democratic U.S. senator from Massachusetts, first elected in 2012; the first woman elected to the Senate from that state
First proposed the idea for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), created by the Dodd–Frank Act of 2010
A Harvard Law School professor and an expert on bankruptcy law
Ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and ended her campaign in March 2020
“Nevertheless, she persisted”: Mitch McConnell’s words after the Senate voted to stop her from speaking in a 2017 debate
Defeated Republican senator Scott Brown in 2012, winning the seat Ted Kennedy had held for decades
In 2017, while the Senate debated Jeff Sessions for attorney general, she read Coretta Scott King’s 1986 letter opposing his nomination as a federal judge
Her 2007 article “Unsafe at Any Rate” said loans and credit cards should be checked for safety, like toasters
Born in Oklahoma City (1949); won a debate scholarship to George Washington University at 16
Wrote _The Two-Income Trap_ (2003) with her daughter, about why middle-class families were going broke
Chaired the Congressional Oversight Panel that watched the bank rescue (TARP) after the 2008 financial crisis
Launched her 2019 presidential campaign in Lawrence, Massachusetts, site of the 1912 “Bread and Roses” strike
Her 2020 campaign became known for the phrase “I have a plan for that”
Barack Obama chose Richard Cordray, not her, as the CFPB’s first director (2011); she then ran for the Senate
Left college to marry, then finished a speech pathology degree at the University of Houston
Taught children with disabilities at a New Jersey public school, then earned a law degree at Rutgers (1976)
Taught law at the University of Texas and the University of Pennsylvania before moving to Harvard
Was registered as a Republican until 1996
Books: _A Fighting Chance_ (2014), _This Fight Is Our Fight_ (2017), and _Persist_ (2021)
While she was growing up in Oklahoma, her father had a heart attack and her mother took a minimum-wage job at Sears
Reelected in 2018 (over Geoff Diehl) and 2024 (over John Deaton)
Proposed a yearly “wealth tax” on households worth more than $50 million during her 2020 campaign

trap.title: Which Warren?
trap.body: Several famous Warrens appear in quiz bowl. Earl Warren was the Chief Justice whose court decided _Brown v. Board of Education_, Robert Penn Warren wrote the novel _All the King’s Men_, and Mercy Otis Warren wrote plays and a history of the American Revolution. Bernie Sanders also ran for the 2020 Democratic nomination, so campaign clues can fit either senator.
trap.fix: Massachusetts, Harvard Law, bankruptcy research, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and “Nevertheless, she persisted” mean Elizabeth Warren. Vermont and Burlington mean Sanders. “Warren” alone is enough on this answer line, but if you add a first name, it must be “Elizabeth.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Elizabeth Warren (accept Elizabeth Ann Warren; prompt on Elizabeth; do not accept “Earl Warren”)

topics.name: Ellis Island
topics.kicker: Immigration station in New York Harbor · About 12 million arrived, 1892–1954
topics.briefing: On January 1, 1892, a teenage girl from Ireland named Annie Moore became the first immigrant processed at a new federal station on a small island in New York Harbor. Over the next 62 years, about 12 million people passed through Ellis Island, waiting in long lines for medical and legal inspections in its Great Hall. Since 1990 its main building has been a museum, and millions of Americans can trace an ancestor who arrived there.
topics.answerHtml: Ellis Island (accept Ellis Island Immigration Station; prompt on Ellis; do not accept “Statue of Liberty,” “Liberty Island,” or “Angel Island”)
accept: ellis island national museum of immigration

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a 1998 case brought by New Jersey against New York, the Supreme Court ruled that the original part of this island belongs to New York, but the much larger area added later with landfill belongs to New Jersey. Landfill had expanded it from about three acres to more than 27.
tossups.r: About 12 million immigrants passed through it. For 10 points, name this island in New York Harbor, once the nation’s busiest immigration station.

tossups.p: Doctors at this place used a small tool called a buttonhook to look under people’s eyelids for trachoma [“truh-KOH-muh”], a contagious eye disease. They marked people who needed a closer exam with chalk letters on their coats, such as “E” for eyes and “H” for heart.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this immigration station near the Statue of Liberty, which opened in 1892.

tossups.p: On June 15, 1897, a fire destroyed this place’s original wooden buildings, though no one was killed. They were replaced in 1900 by a fireproof brick and limestone building with four domed towers, designed by the architects William Boring and Edward Tilton.
tossups.r: Immigrants were inspected in that building’s Great Hall. For 10 points, name this immigration station in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: A teenage girl from County Cork, Ireland, received a ten-dollar gold coin for being the first immigrant processed at this place, on January 1, 1892. Statues of that girl, Annie Moore, stand here and in the Irish port of Cobh [“KOHV”], where her voyage began.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this immigration station in New York Harbor that operated until 1954.

tossups.p: First- and second-class passengers arriving in New York were usually inspected aboard their ships, so most people sent to this place had crossed the ocean in crowded third-class quarters called steerage. Ferries carried them from the docks to this island for inspection.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this immigration station, where about 12 million people arrived between 1892 and 1954.

tossups.p: Immigrants at this place climbed a long staircase to the Registry Room while doctors watched them for signs of illness. Those who passed went down the “Stairs of Separation,” where people bound for trains going west parted from those headed for New York City.
tossups.r: The Registry Room was also called the Great Hall. For 10 points, name this immigration station near the Statue of Liberty.

tossups.p: Before this place opened, New York State had processed immigrants at Castle Garden, an old fort at the southern tip of Manhattan. The national government then took over immigration and opened this station on a small island that had once held a military post called Fort Gibson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal immigration station that opened in New York Harbor in 1892.

tossups.p: In 1916, German agents set off an explosion at the Black Tom munitions depot in nearby Jersey City that shattered windows and damaged buildings at this place. The same blast damaged the arm of the Statue of Liberty that holds the torch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this immigration station in New York Harbor, where about 12 million immigrants arrived.

tossups.p: Historians say it is a myth that officials at this place changed immigrants’ last names, because inspectors worked from passenger lists written at the ports where voyages began. Interpreters helped the inspectors question newcomers in dozens of languages.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this island immigration station, the gateway for about 12 million newcomers to the United States.

tossups.p: After the Immigration Act of 1924 set strict quotas and moved most inspections to American offices overseas, this place was used mainly to hold people waiting to be deported. It closed in 1954, after its last detainee, a Norwegian sailor, was released.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former immigration station in New York Harbor, where Annie Moore had been the first immigrant processed.

tossups.p: In 1965, Lyndon Johnson made this abandoned site part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument. In the 1980s, Chrysler chairman Lee Iacocca [“eye-uh-KOH-kuh”] led a fundraising campaign that paid to restore its main building, which reopened as a museum in 1990.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this island in New York Harbor, a former immigration station.

tossups.p: Photographer Lewis Hine took portraits of newcomers at this place in the early 1900s, before he became famous for photographing child workers. Women and children traveling alone were often held here until a relative arrived to meet them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this immigration station in New York Harbor, which opened in 1892.

tossups.p: In 1907, this place’s busiest year, more than a million immigrants arrived here, and on one April day inspectors processed more than 11,000 people. Most of the newcomers in those years came from southern and eastern Europe, especially Italy, Russia, and Austria-Hungary.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this island immigration station near the Statue of Liberty, where about 12 million people arrived.

tossups.p: Only about two percent of the people who arrived at this place were turned away, often because of contagious diseases or because officials thought they were likely to need public support. It was nicknamed both the “Island of Hope” and the “Island of Tears.”
tossups.r: Doctors there checked newcomers for diseases like trachoma. For 10 points, name this immigration station in New York Harbor.

tossups.p: Families can have an ancestor’s name engraved on the American Immigrant Wall of Honor at this site, whose museum also helps visitors search the passenger lists of ships that arrived in New York. That museum opened in the restored main building in 1990.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former immigration station in New York Harbor, where about 12 million people arrived.

clues.t: The main U.S. immigration station, in New York Harbor, from 1892 to 1954
About 12 million immigrants passed through it
Lies near the Statue of Liberty and has been part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument since 1965
Its main building reopened as an immigration museum in 1990
Annie Moore, a teenager from County Cork, Ireland, was the first immigrant processed (January 1, 1892)
Doctors checked for disease, using buttonhooks to look under eyelids for trachoma
People needing a closer exam were marked with chalk letters, like “E” for eyes and “H” for heart
Inspections took place in the Registry Room, also called the Great Hall
Only about 2 percent were turned away, often for disease or for seeming likely to need public support
_New Jersey v. New York_ (1998): most of the island, built up with landfill, belongs to New Jersey
First- and second-class passengers were inspected on their ships; mostly steerage (third-class) passengers came here
Nicknamed the “Island of Hope” and the “Island of Tears”
A fire destroyed the original wooden buildings in 1897; a fireproof main building opened in 1900
The main building, with four domed towers, was designed by William Boring and Edward Tilton
Replaced Castle Garden, New York State’s immigrant depot at the southern tip of Manhattan
The island once held a military post called Fort Gibson
The 1916 Black Tom explosion in Jersey City, set off by German agents, damaged its buildings and the Statue of Liberty
Myth: officials changed immigrants’ names here; inspectors actually used passenger lists made at the departure ports
Busiest year: 1907, with more than a million arrivals; over 11,000 people were processed on one April day
On the “Stairs of Separation,” people bound for trains going west parted from those headed for New York City
After the 1924 quota law, it served mainly as a detention center; it closed in 1954 after its last detainee, a Norwegian sailor, left
Chrysler chairman Lee Iacocca led the 1980s fundraising campaign to restore it
Lewis Hine photographed immigrants here before his famous photos of child workers
Women and children traveling alone were often held until a relative came to meet them
Annie Moore received a ten-dollar gold coin; statues of her stand on the island and in Cobh, Ireland
The American Immigrant Wall of Honor lists immigrants’ names; the museum helps visitors search ship passenger lists

trap.title: The island next door
trap.body: Ellis Island and Liberty Island, home of the Statue of Liberty, sit close together in New York Harbor and belong to the same national monument, so clues about immigrants arriving by ship can tempt you to say “Statue of Liberty.” Angel Island in San Francisco Bay, sometimes called the “Ellis Island of the West,” was a different immigration station, where many Chinese immigrants were held from 1910 to 1940.
trap.fix: Inspections, doctors with chalk, Annie Moore, the Great Hall, and the years 1892–1954 mean Ellis Island. Emma Lazarus’s poem “The New Colossus,” the sculptor Frédéric Bartholdi, and the torch mean the Statue of Liberty. San Francisco and Chinese immigrants mean Angel Island.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ellis Island (do not accept “Statue of Liberty,” “Liberty Island,” or “Angel Island”)

topics.name: Eminent domain
topics.kicker: Government power to take private property · Requires “just compensation”
topics.briefing: Can the government take your house? Yes, if it needs the land for a public use, like a highway, a school, or a park, and it pays you a fair price. The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause says private property shall not be “taken for public use, without just compensation.” In _Kelo v. City of New London_ (2005), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that a city could take homes for an economic development plan, and many states then passed new limits on this power.
topics.answerHtml: eminent domain (prompt on takings or condemnation; do not accept “Fifth Amendment,” “Takings Clause,” or “zoning”)
reject: kelo v city of new london

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Dutch legal scholar Hugo Grotius [“GROH-shee-us”] coined the Latin name for this power in a 1625 book on the law of war and peace. He argued that a state could take its subjects’ property for public needs, but that it should pay them for what it took.
tossups.r: The Fifth Amendment limits it. For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use.

tossups.p: In a dissent about this power, Sandra Day O’Connor warned that nothing would stop a government from replacing “any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton” or “any home with a shopping mall.” The majority ruled that a Connecticut city’s economic development plan counted as a “public use.”
tossups.r: That 2005 case was _Kelo v. City of New London_. For 10 points, name this power to take private property.

tossups.p: In _Berman v. Parker_, a unanimous Supreme Court let Washington, D.C., use this power on a department store that was not itself run-down, as part of a plan to rebuild a whole neighborhood. William O. Douglas wrote that lawmakers may decide a community should be “beautiful as well as healthy.”
tossups.r: That 1954 decision upheld an urban renewal plan. For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use.

tossups.p: In a 1984 case, the Supreme Court let Hawaii use this power to break up huge estates by moving land from a few large landowners to the people who leased homes on it. Sandra Day O’Connor wrote that opinion, though she later dissented in a famous case about the same power.
tossups.r: That later case was _Kelo v. City of New London_. For 10 points, name this government power, which the Fifth Amendment limits.

tossups.p: In 1857, New York City used this power to remove the residents of Seneca Village, a community where many African American families owned land, to make room for Central Park. The landowners were paid for their property, as the law required.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of a government to take private property for public use if it pays the owner.

tossups.p: In an 1897 case about a railroad’s land in Chicago, the Supreme Court ruled that states, not just the national government, must pay “just compensation” when they use this power. That decision is often called the first to apply part of the Bill of Rights to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
tossups.r: That case involved the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad. For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use.

tossups.p: In 1981, Michigan’s top court let Detroit use this power to clear a neighborhood called Poletown so that General Motors could build a car factory. The same court reversed itself in 2004, ruling that taking property just to boost the economy broke the state’s constitution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of governments to take private land for public use, if they pay for it.

tossups.p: New York planner Robert Moses used this power to clear land for highways such as the Cross Bronx Expressway, forcing thousands of people to move. In the 1950s and 1960s, many cities also used it for “urban renewal” projects that tore down older neighborhoods.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this government power to take private property in exchange for “just compensation.”

tossups.p: In _Kohl v. United States_ (1875), the Supreme Court ruled that the national government itself could use this power, in a case about land for federal offices in Cincinnati. Courts call the legal process of using this power “condemnation.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of a government to take private property for public use.

tossups.p: After a 2005 Supreme Court decision about this power, dozens of states passed laws limiting it, and the land at the center of the case stayed empty for years. Supporters of the ruling said it let cities rebuild struggling economies, while critics said it put ordinary people’s homes at risk.
tossups.r: That case was _Kelo v. City of New London_. For 10 points, name this government power to take private property.

tossups.p: Susette Kelo’s “little pink house,” which a Connecticut city wanted for a development plan near a Pfizer research center, became a symbol in a fight over this power. After she lost her case, the house was moved to another spot in the city.
tossups.r: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 against her in 2005. For 10 points, name this power of governments to take private property.

tossups.p: In the 1950s, Los Angeles used this power to clear Chavez Ravine, a mostly Mexican American neighborhood, for a public housing project that was later canceled. The land was then used to build Dodger Stadium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use, as long as the owner is fairly paid.

tossups.p: The Tennessee Valley Authority used this power in the 1930s to acquire farms that would be flooded by its new dams, and states later used it to build the Interstate Highway System. In each case, owners had to be paid for their land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use, which the Takings Clause limits.

tossups.p: The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 promised “a reasonable compensation” to anyone whose property was taken for public uses, an early limit on this power. A national limit followed in 1791, when the Bill of Rights was ratified.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this government power to take private property for public use, which the Fifth Amendment says requires “just compensation.”

tossups.p: In the 1800s, many states let private canal and railroad companies use this power to get land for their routes, on the grounds that those projects served the public. Utility companies have also used it to build power lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power to take private property for public use, as long as the owner receives “just compensation.”

clues.t: The government’s power to take private property for public use
Limited by the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause: property may not be taken “for public use, without just compensation”
Used to get land for highways, schools, parks, dams, and railroads
_Kelo v. City of New London_ (2005): the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that a city could take homes for an economic development plan
“Just compensation” usually means the property’s fair market value
The legal process of using it is called condemnation
Sandra Day O’Connor’s _Kelo_ dissent: nothing stops replacing “any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton”
_Berman v. Parker_ (1954): a unanimous ruling upheld a D.C. urban renewal plan; William O. Douglas: “beautiful as well as healthy”
Supporters said _Kelo_ helped cities rebuild struggling economies; critics said it put homes at risk; dozens of states then limited such takings
Susette Kelo’s “little pink house” in Connecticut became a symbol of the case
Used in 1950s–1960s “urban renewal” and by Robert Moses for highways like the Cross Bronx Expressway
Hugo Grotius coined its Latin name in a 1625 book on the law of war and peace
_Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff_ (1984): O’Connor’s opinion let Hawaii break up large estates
An 1897 Chicago railroad case required states to pay too; often called the first case applying part of the Bill of Rights to the states
_Kohl v. United States_ (1875): the national government may use it too
New York City used it in 1857 to remove Seneca Village, a largely African American community, for Central Park
Michigan’s _Poletown_ ruling (1981) let Detroit clear a neighborhood for a General Motors plant; reversed in 2004
Los Angeles cleared Chavez Ravine in the 1950s; the land became the site of Dodger Stadium
The Tennessee Valley Authority used it for land flooded by its dams; states used it for the Interstate Highway System
The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 promised “a reasonable compensation”
In the 1800s, states let private canal and railroad companies use it
The _Kelo_ plan was tied to a Pfizer research center; the land stayed empty for years

trap.title: The power, not the amendment
trap.body: Almost every tossup on this power mentions the Fifth Amendment, its Takings Clause, or “just compensation,” and those words tempt early buzzes. But the Fifth Amendment does not create this power; it limits it by requiring payment, so naming the amendment or the clause answers a different question and is ruled wrong here. Zoning, which controls how land may be used without taking it, is also wrong.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this power” or “this practice” of taking property for public use, say “eminent domain.” Save “Fifth Amendment” for “this amendment” and “Takings Clause” for “this clause.” Saying only “takings” or “condemnation” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: eminent domain (prompt on takings or condemnation; do not accept “Fifth Amendment” or “zoning”)

topics.name: Environmental Protection Agency
topics.kicker: Federal agency that enforces pollution laws · Created under Nixon in 1970
topics.briefing: In 1969, an oil-soaked river in Cleveland caught fire, drawing national attention to pollution. The next year, about 20 million Americans took part in the first Earth Day, and President Richard Nixon created the Environmental Protection Agency to enforce national rules on clean air and water. Led first by William Ruckelshaus, the EPA soon banned most uses of the pesticide DDT, which Rachel Carson had warned about in her 1962 book _Silent Spring_.
topics.answerHtml: Environmental Protection Agency (or EPA; do not accept “Department of the Interior” or a law it enforces, such as the “Clean Air Act”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This agency was created not by a new act of Congress but by Reorganization Plan No. 3, which combined offices from the Departments of the Interior, Agriculture, and Health, Education, and Welfare. It opened in December 1970, months after the first Earth Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that Richard Nixon set up to fight pollution.

tossups.p: This agency’s first leader later resigned as deputy attorney general rather than fire Watergate prosecutor Archibald Cox during the “Saturday Night Massacre.” That man, William Ruckelshaus [“RUCK-ulz-howss”], returned to lead this agency again in the 1980s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency, created in 1970, that enforces the Clean Air Act.

tossups.p: After months of hearings, this agency’s first head overruled a hearing examiner and in 1972 banned most uses of a pesticide that had thinned the eggshells of bald eagles and brown pelicans.
tossups.r: That pesticide, DDT, had been the focus of Rachel Carson’s _Silent Spring_. For 10 points, name this agency created in 1970.

tossups.p: Families were moved out of the Love Canal neighborhood of Niagara Falls, New York, after chemical waste was found buried beneath their homes and a school. In response, Congress passed a 1980 law that set up a “Superfund” for this agency to clean up toxic waste sites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that enforces pollution laws and is known by a three-letter abbreviation.

tossups.p: In 1972, Congress overrode Richard Nixon’s veto to pass the Clean Water Act, which this agency enforces. Support for that law had grown after Cleveland’s Cuyahoga [“ky-uh-HOH-guh”] River, covered with oil and waste, caught fire in 1969.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that Nixon had created to fight pollution.

tossups.p: In a 2007 case brought by Massachusetts against this agency, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that carbon dioxide from new cars counts as an air pollutant that this agency has the power to regulate under the Clean Air Act.
tossups.r: Its first leader was William Ruckelshaus. For 10 points, name this federal agency created under Richard Nixon in 1970.

tossups.p: Rules set by this agency led carmakers to add catalytic converters starting with 1975 models, which meant those cars had to use unleaded gasoline. Lead was later banned from gasoline for cars entirely, starting in 1996.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that enforces the Clean Air Act and was created under Richard Nixon.

tossups.p: In 1992, this agency started the Energy Star program, which labels computers, appliances, and other products that use less energy. Under the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1974, it also sets limits on harmful substances in public tap water.
tossups.r: It also runs the Superfund program for toxic waste sites. For 10 points, name this federal agency created under Richard Nixon.

tossups.p: Under the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which George H. W. Bush signed, this agency began a program that let power plants buy and sell permits to release sulfur dioxide, a cause of acid rain. That “cap-and-trade” system sharply cut sulfur dioxide pollution.
tossups.r: This agency also banned most uses of DDT in 1972. For 10 points, name this federal agency that Richard Nixon created in 1970.

tossups.p: Wisconsin senator Gaylord Nelson organized a nationwide day of teach-ins about pollution on April 22, 1970, which about 20 million Americans joined. In December of that year, this new federal agency opened its doors.
tossups.r: That April day was the first Earth Day. For 10 points, name this agency that Richard Nixon created.

tossups.p: This agency reviews the environmental impact statements that a law signed on January 1, 1970, requires for major federal projects. That law, the National Environmental Policy Act, also created a White House Council on Environmental Quality.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agency, created later in 1970, that enforces the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act.

tossups.p: In 1983, this agency agreed to buy out the entire town of Times Beach, Missouri, after a chemical called dioxin was found in oil that had been sprayed on its dirt roads to keep down dust. The town’s site later became a state park.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that runs the Superfund cleanup program and enforces the Clean Air Act.

tossups.p: After a 1984 gas leak at a chemical plant killed thousands of people in Bhopal, India, Congress passed a 1986 law requiring factories to report the toxic chemicals they release. This agency publishes those reports in the Toxics Release Inventory.
tossups.r: It also enforces the Clean Water Act. For 10 points, name this federal agency founded in 1970 under Richard Nixon.

tossups.p: A 1962 book that opens with “A Fable for Tomorrow,” about an imaginary American town where the birds have stopped singing, helped start the movement that led to this agency. Its author, a former government biologist, died two years after it was published.
tossups.r: That book was Rachel Carson’s _Silent Spring_. For 10 points, name this agency created in 1970 to fight pollution.

tossups.p: Less than a month after this agency opened, a 1970 law ordered it to set national air-quality standards for common pollutants such as carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide. The same law required large cuts in the exhaust from new cars.
tossups.r: That law was the Clean Air Act. For 10 points, name this agency that Richard Nixon created.

clues.t: Created by President Richard Nixon in 1970; it opened that December
The federal agency that enforces national pollution laws like the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act
Banned most uses of the pesticide DDT in 1972
Inspired in part by Rachel Carson’s _Silent Spring_ (1962), a book about the dangers of pesticides
First administrator: William Ruckelshaus (1970–1973, and again 1983–1985)
Created the same year as the first Earth Day (April 22, 1970), organized by Senator Gaylord Nelson
Runs the Superfund program (1980), which cleans up toxic waste sites
Love Canal, a Niagara Falls neighborhood built over buried chemical waste, led to the Superfund law
Cleveland’s Cuyahoga River caught fire in 1969, building support for clean water laws
Congress overrode Nixon’s veto to pass the Clean Water Act (1972)
Created by Reorganization Plan No. 3, which combined offices from Interior, Agriculture, and Health, Education, and Welfare
Ruckelshaus later resigned as deputy attorney general in the Saturday Night Massacre (1973)
Ruckelshaus banned DDT after months of hearings, overruling a hearing examiner; DDT had thinned the eggshells of eagles and pelicans
A 2007 case brought by Massachusetts: the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that it may regulate carbon dioxide from new cars
Its rules brought catalytic converters (1975 models) and unleaded gasoline; leaded gas for cars was banned starting in 1996
Started the Energy Star label for energy-saving products (1992)
1990 Clean Air Act amendments: a cap-and-trade program for sulfur dioxide to fight acid rain
Reviews the environmental impact statements required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), signed January 1, 1970
Bought out Times Beach, Missouri (1983), after dioxin was found in oil sprayed on its roads
Publishes the Toxics Release Inventory, created by a 1986 law passed after the Bhopal disaster in India
_Silent Spring_ opens with “A Fable for Tomorrow,” about a town where the birds no longer sing; Carson died in 1964
Sets limits on harmful substances in tap water under the Safe Drinking Water Act (1974)
The Clean Air Act of 1970 ordered it to set national air-quality standards for pollutants like carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide

trap.title: Agency, not a law
trap.body: Most tossups on this agency name the laws it enforces, like the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and Superfund, or events that led to it, like the first Earth Day and Rachel Carson’s _Silent Spring_. Those are separate answer lines, so blurting out a law or an event when the question asks for “this agency” loses the tossup. The Department of the Interior, which runs the National Park Service, is a different part of the government.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this agency” with Richard Nixon, William Ruckelshaus, the DDT ban, or Love Canal wants the Environmental Protection Agency, and “EPA” is fine. “This law” wants the specific act, and “this day” wants Earth Day.

topics.name: Equal Rights Amendment
topics.kicker: Proposed amendment for equal rights regardless of sex · Passed Congress in 1972
topics.briefing: Alice Paul, who had helped win women the right to vote, wrote the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 to guarantee equal rights under the law regardless of sex. Congress passed it in 1972, but by its 1982 deadline only 35 of the 38 states needed had approved it, as opponents led by Phyllis Schlafly campaigned against it. Nevada, Illinois, and Virginia voted to ratify it decades later, and whether those late votes count has been debated in Congress and the courts.
topics.answerHtml: Equal Rights Amendment (or ERA; accept Lucretia Mott Amendment or Alice Paul Amendment; prompt on equal rights; do not accept “Nineteenth Amendment” or “Fourteenth Amendment”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In December 1923, Senator Charles Curtis, a future vice president, and Representative Daniel Anthony, a nephew of Susan B. Anthony, first introduced this proposal in Congress. Its author had announced it months earlier at Seneca Falls, New York.
tossups.r: That author, Alice Paul, led the National Woman’s Party. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that Congress finally passed in 1972.

tossups.p: In 1943, this proposal’s author rewrote it to sound like the amendment that had given women the vote, saying that “equality of rights under the law” could not be “denied or abridged” on account of sex. The proposal was then renamed for its author.
tossups.r: That author was Alice Paul. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that was three states short of ratification when its 1982 deadline passed.

tossups.p: In 1970, Michigan congresswoman Martha Griffiths used a discharge petition to force this proposal out of a House committee where it had been stuck for decades. After the House approved it again in 1971, the Senate followed in March 1972.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that would forbid denying rights under the law on account of sex.

tossups.p: Hawaii approved this proposal within hours of its passage by Congress in March 1972. Congress placed a seven-year deadline for ratification in the resolution’s opening words rather than in the text of the amendment itself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that only 35 states had ratified when its deadline arrived.

tossups.p: Phyllis Schlafly led opposition to this proposal through a group whose name stood for “Stop Taking Our Privileges.” She argued that it could take away protections women had, such as being exempt from the military draft, while supporters said it would guarantee equal treatment under the law.
tossups.r: Alice Paul had first written it in 1923. For 10 points, name this proposed constitutional amendment, which Congress passed in 1972.

tossups.p: After ratifications of this proposal stalled at 35 states in 1977, Congress voted the next year to extend its deadline from March 1979 to June 30, 1982. No more states approved it before the new deadline, and several states had voted to withdraw their earlier approvals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment, written by Alice Paul, that needed approval from 38 states to be ratified.

tossups.p: In January 2020, Virginia became the 38th state to vote to ratify this proposal, following Nevada in 2017 and Illinois in 2018. Because those votes came long after the deadline Congress had set, the Archivist of the United States did not certify it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment, first written by Alice Paul in 1923 and passed by Congress in 1972.

tossups.p: In January 2025, President Joe Biden said he considered this proposal part of the Constitution, but the Archivist of the United States said it could not be certified, citing earlier legal and court decisions about its deadline. Supporters and opponents had argued for years over whether late approvals counted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that Congress passed in 1972 with a seven-year ratification deadline.

tossups.p: This proposal’s author announced it in July 1923 at Seneca Falls, New York, during a celebration of the 75th anniversary of the first women’s rights convention held there. She named it for one of that convention’s organizers, Lucretia Mott.
tossups.r: That author was Alice Paul. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that would ban denying rights on account of sex.

tossups.p: The second section of this proposal lets Congress enforce it with laws, and the third says it would take effect two years after ratification. Its first section bars denying “equality of rights under the law” on account of sex.
tossups.r: Alice Paul first wrote it in 1923. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that Congress passed in 1972.

tossups.p: Opponents of this proposal brought loaves of homemade bread to state legislators, in a campaign led by the founder of the conservative group Eagle Forum. Many of those opponents described themselves as homemakers.
tossups.r: That founder was Phyllis Schlafly. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that was not ratified by 38 states before its 1982 deadline.

tossups.p: In July 1978, about 100,000 people marched in Washington, D.C., to ask Congress to give this proposal more time. The National Organization for Women had made winning its ratification one of the group’s top goals.
tossups.r: Congress agreed, extending the deadline to 1982. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment written by Alice Paul.

tossups.p: Nebraska approved this proposal in 1972 and then voted in 1973 to take back its approval, the first of several states to do so. Whether a state may withdraw a ratification has been debated ever since.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment, which Congress sent to the states in 1972.

tossups.p: In 1940, the Republican Party became the first major party to support this proposal in its platform, and the Democrats followed four years later. Republicans removed that support from their platform in 1980.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this proposed amendment, which Congress passed in 1972 and which Phyllis Schlafly campaigned against.

tossups.p: For decades, some labor reformers opposed this proposal because they feared it would wipe out laws that limited women’s working hours and protected women in factories. Its supporters in the National Woman’s Party answered that such laws kept women out of many jobs.
tossups.r: Congress finally passed it in 1972. For 10 points, name this proposed amendment that Alice Paul wrote in 1923.

clues.t: Written by Alice Paul of the National Woman’s Party in 1923
Passed by Congress in 1972 and sent to the states with a seven-year deadline
Only 35 states had ratified by the deadline, three short of the 38 needed
Phyllis Schlafly led the opposition through a campaign called STOP (“Stop Taking Our Privileges”)
Key words: “Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged … on account of sex”
Congress extended the deadline from 1979 to June 30, 1982, but no more states ratified
Virginia voted to ratify in January 2020 as the 38th state, after Nevada (2017) and Illinois (2018)
The Archivist of the United States did not certify it, citing the expired deadline
Alice Paul announced it at Seneca Falls in 1923, on the 75th anniversary of the women’s rights convention there
Originally named for Lucretia Mott; reworded in 1943 and renamed for its author
Several states, starting with Nebraska in 1973, voted to take back (rescind) their approvals
Opponents argued it could end women’s exemption from the military draft; supporters said it would guarantee equal treatment
First introduced in Congress in December 1923 by Senator Charles Curtis and Representative Daniel Anthony, Susan B. Anthony’s nephew
Martha Griffiths of Michigan used a discharge petition (1970) to get it out of a House committee
Hawaii was the first state to ratify, within hours of the Senate’s vote in March 1972
The deadline was placed in the resolution’s opening words, not in the amendment’s text
Indiana was the 35th state, in 1977; no other state voted to ratify until Nevada in 2017
In January 2025, President Joe Biden said he considered it part of the Constitution; the Archivist said it could not be certified
Section 2 lets Congress enforce it; Section 3 says it takes effect two years after ratification
Schlafly founded the conservative group Eagle Forum; opponents brought homemade bread to state legislators
About 100,000 people marched in Washington in July 1978 for more time; the National Organization for Women made it a top goal
Republicans backed it in their platform from 1940 until 1980; Democrats backed it starting in 1944
Some labor reformers opposed it for decades, fearing it would end laws that limited women’s working hours

trap.title: Which women’s amendment?
trap.body: Two amendments about women come up constantly. The Nineteenth Amendment (1920), nicknamed the Susan B. Anthony Amendment, says the right to vote cannot be denied on account of sex; this proposal, written by Alice Paul in 1923, would bar denying equal rights under the law on account of sex. Because Alice Paul also led protests for the vote, early clues about her can fit either answer, and the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause is a third trap.
trap.fix: Voting, 1920, and the Silent Sentinels mean the Nineteenth Amendment. Phyllis Schlafly, 1972, a ratification deadline, 35 states, or Virginia in 2020 mean the Equal Rights Amendment, and “ERA” is fine. “Equal protection of the laws” and Reconstruction mean the Fourteenth.
trap.line: Real answer line: Equal Rights Amendment (or ERA; do not accept “Nineteenth Amendment”)

topics.name: Federal Reserve System
topics.kicker: The central bank of the United States · Created in 1913 under Woodrow Wilson
topics.briefing: During a banking panic in 1907, the financier J. P. Morgan gathered other bankers to stop the crisis, and afterward Congress decided the country needed a central bank. The Federal Reserve Act, signed by Woodrow Wilson in 1913, created a system of 12 regional banks overseen by a board in Washington. The Fed controls the supply of money and raises or lowers interest rates to keep prices steady and help people find jobs.
topics.answerHtml: Federal Reserve System (or the Fed; accept Federal Reserve Board or Federal Reserve Banks; prompt on central bank or Federal Reserve Act; do not accept “Treasury” or “Bank of the United States”)
accept: board of governors of the federal reserve
reject: first bank of the united states
second bank of the united states

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In November 1910, Senator Nelson Aldrich met secretly with a Treasury official and several leading bankers at a hunting club on Jekyll Island, Georgia, where they posed as duck hunters while drafting a plan that led to this institution. Their meeting stayed secret for years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, created by a 1913 law.

tossups.p: Virginia congressman Carter Glass and Oklahoma senator Robert Owen sponsored the law that created this institution, which Woodrow Wilson signed two days before Christmas in 1913. That law set up a system of twelve regional banks.
tossups.r: Its chairs have included Alan Greenspan and Ben Bernanke. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: Missouri is the only state with two of this institution’s regional banks, one in St. Louis and one in Kansas City. Its other regional banks are in cities such as Boston, Atlanta, Minneapolis, Dallas, and San Francisco.
tossups.r: Its Board of Governors meets in Washington, D.C. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: After the Panic of 1907, the Aldrich–Vreeland Act set up a National Monetary Commission to study banking, and that commission’s work eventually led to this institution. During the panic, J. P. Morgan had gathered bankers in his library to stop the spreading crisis.
tossups.r: Congress created this institution in 1913 to help prevent such panics. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: Chairman Paul Volcker led this institution to push short-term interest rates to nearly 20 percent around 1980 to fight the high inflation of the 1970s, and the economy went through a sharp recession. Jimmy Carter had appointed him in 1979.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, later led from 2006 to 2014 by Ben Bernanke.

tossups.p: The twelve voting members of this institution’s main policy committee are seven governors, the president of its New York bank, and four other regional bank presidents who take turns. That committee meets eight times a year to set a target for a key short-term interest rate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, whose policy committee is the Federal Open Market Committee.

tossups.p: The Banking Act of 1935 reorganized this institution and gave more power to its board in Washington, which meets in a building named for its chair at the time, Marriner Eccles. Eccles had been a Utah banker before joining Franklin Roosevelt’s administration.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, created in 1913 under Woodrow Wilson.

tossups.p: In a 1996 speech, this institution’s chairman asked whether “irrational exuberance” had pushed stock prices too high. That chairman, who served from 1987 to 2006, had taken office just two months before the Black Monday stock market crash.
tossups.r: That chairman was Alan Greenspan. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: This institution’s San Francisco bank was led from 2004 to 2010 by an economist who then became its vice chair in 2010 and who later served as secretary of the Treasury from 2021 to 2025.
tossups.r: That economist, Janet Yellen, became the first woman to chair this institution. For 10 points, name this central bank, which Jerome Powell began leading in 2018.

tossups.p: A 1977 law gave this institution its “dual mandate” to aim for both maximum employment and stable prices, and a 1978 law named for Hubert Humphrey and Augustus Hawkins requires its chair to report to Congress twice a year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank that raises interest rates to fight inflation and lowers them during recessions.

tossups.p: Eight times a year, this institution publishes the Beige Book, a summary of business conditions gathered by each of its twelve regional banks. Those banks are numbered by district, from the First District in Boston to the Twelfth in San Francisco.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, whose chair from 2006 to 2014 was Ben Bernanke.

tossups.p: In _A Monetary History of the United States_, Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed this institution for making the Great Depression worse by letting the money supply shrink by about a third. In 2002, Ben Bernanke told them, “We did it. We’re very sorry.”
tossups.r: Bernanke later chaired this institution from 2006 to 2014. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: This institution’s New York bank buys and sells government bonds in “open market operations” to change how much money banks have to lend. It can also lend money directly to banks through its “discount window.”
tossups.r: Its name appears on U.S. paper bills. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States, created in 1913.

tossups.p: William McChesney Martin, this institution’s longest-serving chairman, compared its job to a chaperone who orders the punch bowl taken away just as the party is warming up. Martin took charge in 1951, soon after an accord freed this institution from holding down interest rates for the Treasury.
tossups.r: Later chairs included Paul Volcker and Alan Greenspan. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

tossups.p: In December 2008, this institution cut its target for short-term interest rates to nearly zero, and starting in late 2008 it bought huge amounts of bonds in a program called “quantitative easing.” Months earlier, it had made an emergency loan to the insurance company AIG.
tossups.r: Its chairman at the time was Ben Bernanke. For 10 points, name this central bank of the United States.

clues.t: The central bank of the United States
Raises interest rates to fight inflation and lowers them to help the economy grow
Created by a 1913 law signed by Woodrow Wilson
A system of 12 regional banks overseen by a Board of Governors in Washington, D.C.
Chairs include Alan Greenspan (1987–2006), Ben Bernanke (2006–2014), and Janet Yellen (2014–2018), the first woman
Controls the money supply; its name appears on U.S. paper bills
The Federal Open Market Committee sets its interest-rate target and meets eight times a year
Paul Volcker (chair 1979–1987) pushed interest rates to nearly 20 percent to fight inflation
Its seven governors are appointed by the president, confirmed by the Senate, and serve 14-year terms
The Panic of 1907, which J. P. Morgan helped stop, convinced Congress that a central bank was needed
Jerome Powell became chair in 2018, succeeding Janet Yellen
“Dual mandate” from a 1977 law: maximum employment and stable prices
Planned at a secret 1910 meeting on Jekyll Island, Georgia, by Senator Nelson Aldrich and leading bankers posing as duck hunters
The 1913 law was sponsored by Representative Carter Glass and Senator Robert Owen
Missouri is the only state with two of its regional banks (St. Louis and Kansas City)
The Banking Act of 1935 strengthened its board; its headquarters is named for chair Marriner Eccles
Alan Greenspan’s 1996 “irrational exuberance” speech; he took office two months before the 1987 Black Monday crash
Publishes the Beige Book, a summary of conditions in its 12 districts, eight times a year
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed it for letting the money supply shrink during the Great Depression
Classic tools: open market operations (buying and selling government bonds), the discount window, and reserve requirements
William McChesney Martin (1951–1970), the longest-serving chair, said its job was to take away the punch bowl as the party warms up
A 1951 accord with the Treasury Department freed it from holding down interest rates
In late 2008 it cut rates to nearly zero and began “quantitative easing” bond purchases; it also made an emergency loan to AIG
The Humphrey–Hawkins Act (1978) requires the chair to report to Congress twice a year
Janet Yellen led its San Francisco bank (2004–2010) and later served as Treasury secretary (2021–2025)

trap.title: Fed, Treasury, or Bank?
trap.body: Three money institutions get mixed up. The Department of the Treasury collects taxes, borrows money for the government, and makes coins and paper bills; the First and Second Banks of the United States were earlier national banks whose charters ran out in 1811 and 1836; and this central bank, created in 1913, sets interest rates and controls the money supply. Clues about Treasury secretaries or Andrew Jackson’s Bank War can pull you toward the wrong one.
trap.fix: If you hear 1913, Jekyll Island, 12 regional banks, the Federal Open Market Committee, or chairs like Volcker, Greenspan, Bernanke, and Yellen, say “Federal Reserve”; “the Fed” is fine too. Alexander Hamilton (1791) or Nicholas Biddle and Andrew Jackson mean a Bank of the United States.
trap.line: Real answer line: Federal Reserve System (or the Fed; prompt on central bank; do not accept “Treasury”)

topics.name: Federalism
topics.kicker: Sharing power between the nation and the states · Built into the Constitution
topics.briefing: Who makes the rules where you live: your state or the national government? Under federalism, the answer is both. The Constitution gives some powers, like coining money and declaring war, to the national government and leaves many others, like running schools, mostly to the states, and the Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people the powers not given to the nation. When state and national laws clash, the Supremacy Clause says national law wins.
topics.answerHtml: federalism (accept federal system; accept dual, cooperative, or New federalism; prompt on division of powers; do not accept “Federalist Party,” “Federalist Papers,” “checks and balances,” or “separation of powers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Dissenting in _New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann_ in 1932, Louis Brandeis wrote that “a single courageous State may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory” and try “novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.”
tossups.r: That idea is summed up as “laboratories of democracy.” For 10 points, name this system of sharing power between the national government and the states.

tossups.p: James Madison wrote that in “the compound republic of America,” power is first divided between “two distinct governments” and then split among separate branches, so that “a double security arises to the rights of the people.”
tossups.r: Those two levels are the national and state governments. For 10 points, name this principle of dividing power between them.

tossups.p: In _Federalist_ No. 45, James Madison promised that the powers given to the new national government would be “few and defined,” while those left to the states would be “numerous and indefinite.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system, protected by the Tenth Amendment, that divides power between the nation and the states.

tossups.p: Political scientist Morton Grodzins compared one form of this principle to a marble cake, in which national, state, and local governments mix their work together, unlike an older “layer cake” model in which each level kept to its own jobs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that divides power between the national government and the states.

tossups.p: Richard Nixon’s revenue-sharing program and Ronald Reagan’s block grants were part of a “new” version of this principle, which aimed to shift money and decision-making from Washington to state and local governments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system of dividing power between the national government and the states, protected by the Tenth Amendment.

tossups.p: In an 1819 case about a tax on the Second Bank of the United States, John Marshall ruled that the national government is supreme within its own sphere and that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy,” so a state could not tax the bank.
tossups.r: That case, _McCulloch v. Maryland_, helped define this division of power. For 10 points, name this principle of sharing power between the nation and the states.

tossups.p: In _New York v. United States_ (1992), Sandra Day O’Connor wrote for the Supreme Court that Congress could not force states to take ownership of radioactive waste, because the national government may not simply order state governments to carry out its programs.
tossups.r: That ruling relied on the Tenth Amendment. For 10 points, name this system that divides power between the national government and the states.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Lopez_ (1995), the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in nearly sixty years that Congress had gone beyond its power to regulate commerce among the states, striking down a law that banned guns near schools.
tossups.r: Rulings like that one shape this system. For 10 points, name this division of power between the national and state governments.

tossups.p: Under the doctrine of preemption, a valid act of Congress overrides a conflicting state law, and judges in every state must follow it. That rule comes from a clause in Article VI of the Constitution.
tossups.r: That Supremacy Clause makes national law “the supreme Law of the Land.” For 10 points, name this system of sharing power between the nation and the states.

tossups.p: Under the Articles of Confederation, the states kept most power, and the national Congress could not collect taxes or regulate trade. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787, the framers created a stronger national government while keeping the states, a balance at the heart of this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that divides power between the national government and the states.

tossups.p: Powers held by both levels of government in this system, such as taxing and borrowing money, are called concurrent powers. Powers given only to the national government, such as coining money and declaring war, are called delegated or enumerated powers.
tossups.r: Powers kept by the states are called reserved powers. For 10 points, name this system of dividing power between the nation and the states.

tossups.p: John C. Calhoun argued that a state could nullify a national law it judged unconstitutional, and in 1832 South Carolina declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void. Andrew Jackson answered with the Force Bill, and a compromise tariff ended the crisis in 1833.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system of sharing power between the nation and the states, which that Nullification Crisis tested.

tossups.p: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798, arguing that states could judge whether national laws such as the Alien and Sedition Acts went beyond the powers the Constitution granted.
tossups.r: Those resolutions argued for the states’ side of this system. For 10 points, name this division of power between the national government and the states.

tossups.p: In _South Dakota v. Dole_ (1987), the Supreme Court let Congress withhold some highway money from states that kept their drinking age below 21. Such conditions on grants of money are one way the national government shapes state policy in this system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system that divides power between the national and state governments.

tossups.p: In _Hammer v. Dagenhart_ (1918), the Supreme Court struck down a national law against child labor, ruling that factory work was for the states, not Congress, to regulate. That decision reflected a strict “layer cake” view of this system that lasted until the New Deal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this system of dividing power between the national government and the states.

clues.t: The division of power between the national government and the state governments
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not given to the national government to the states or the people
Article VI’s Supremacy Clause: national law wins when it conflicts with state law
Replaced the weak national government of the Articles of Confederation with a new balance in the 1787 Constitution
Delegated (enumerated) powers belong to the nation, reserved powers to the states, and concurrent powers, like taxing, to both
Louis Brandeis (1932): a state may “serve as a laboratory” for new ideas, the source of the phrase “laboratories of democracy”
“Layer cake” (dual) model vs. “marble cake” (cooperative) model, a comparison made by Morton Grodzins
_McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819): a state cannot tax the national bank; “the power to tax involves the power to destroy”
_Federalist_ No. 45 (Madison): national powers are “few and defined,” state powers “numerous and indefinite”
John C. Calhoun’s idea of nullification and South Carolina’s Nullification Crisis (1832–1833) tested it
Nixon’s revenue sharing and Reagan’s block grants tried to shift money and power back to the states
Differs from a unitary system, where the central government holds most power, and a confederation, where the states do
_Federalist_ No. 51: the “compound republic” divides power between “two distinct governments,” a “double security” for rights
Brandeis’s line came from his dissent in _New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann_ (1932)
_New York v. United States_ (1992): Congress may not force states to take ownership of radioactive waste
_United States v. Lopez_ (1995): the first limit on Congress’s commerce power in nearly 60 years
_South Dakota v. Dole_ (1987): Congress may withhold highway money from states with a drinking age under 21
_Hammer v. Dagenhart_ (1918): struck down a national child-labor law as a matter for the states
The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (1798), by Jefferson and Madison, said states could judge national laws
Andrew Jackson’s Force Bill and the Compromise Tariff of 1833 ended the Nullification Crisis
Grants-in-aid: national money given to states, often with conditions (“strings attached”)
The “anti-commandeering” rule: the national government cannot force state officials to carry out its programs
Preemption: a valid act of Congress overrides a conflicting state law

trap.title: Not the Federalists
trap.body: Several answer lines sound like this one. The Federalist Party was the party of Alexander Hamilton and John Adams in the 1790s, and _The Federalist Papers_ were 85 essays defending the Constitution, so saying either one for this principle is wrong. It is also easy to confuse with the separation of powers and checks and balances, which divide power among the three branches, not between levels of government.
trap.fix: If the clue is about the nation versus the states (the Tenth Amendment, the Supremacy Clause, _McCulloch v. Maryland_, layer and marble cakes, or “laboratories of democracy”), say “federalism.” If it is about the president, Congress, and the courts limiting one another, think checks and balances or the separation of powers.
trap.line: Real answer line: federalism (accept federal system; do not accept “Federalist Party,” “checks and balances,” or “separation of powers”)
